utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. Judge Van den Wyngaert, unfortunately, is not well, and will be unable, we expect to sit throughout the day, so other two Judges will sit under the Rule. Could I remind you of the affirmation again, Mr. Bushi, which applies still. Ms. Regue.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Could we please call Exhibit 1D236. It was former 65 ter 1D117. And if we could go to the first page.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Mr. Bushi, I'm going to show to you a document that was shown by my colleague. It's an order, an executive order 13219 dated June 26, of 2001, issued by the president of the United States. The title is: "Blocking property of persons who threaten international stabilisation efforts in the Western Balkans." Do you recall being shown this document, Mr. Bushi? It's, unfortunately, only in English.

utterances.speaker: NAZIM BUSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall it.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: I'm just going to read to you a couple of extracts to refresh your memory. I quote: "I, George W. Bush," this is in the second paragraph, "president of the United States of America have determined that the actions of persons engaged in or assisting, sponsoring or supporting extremist violence in the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia and then some restrictive measures with regards to property, with regards to assets of individuals are indicated. And these individuals are the persons listed in annex -- in the annex of this order, and persons designated by the secretary of the treasury that have committed or to pose a significant risk of committing acts of violence but have the purpose or effect of threatening the peace in, or diminishing the stability of any area or state in the western Balkan region." If we go to page number 4 of this document we see the annex with the list of persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: To page number 4. Thanks. If we could scroll up a little bit you see that there are two columns. One with individuals, the name; and the second column reads affiliations. The second name that you see is Ali Ahmeti and the affiliations, NLA. Are you able to see that, Mr. Bushi?

utterances.speaker: NAZIM BUSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: For instance the fourth name is Dalipi Tahir and the affiliations is PCPMB. Do you see that, Mr. Bushi?

utterances.speaker: NAZIM BUSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: If could you go to the next page, please. We see here more names, and also different affiliations and then the second point is affiliations, their organisations are listed with the full -- with the full characters. Mr. Bushi, in this list, did you see all the names of all the individuals who belong to the NLA?

utterances.speaker: NAZIM BUSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There aren't all the names here. There are only some of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Did you see names of individuals of persons belonging to other organisations?

utterances.speaker: NAZIM BUSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: At any time in the extracts that I read to you or next to affiliation, have you heard or did you read that the NLA was defined as a foreign terrorist organisation by the US government?

utterances.speaker: NAZIM BUSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nowhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will refer to this point, to the testimony of Peter Bouckaert, pages 3179, 3227, and 3231. If we could go to Exhibit 1D230, please. It's former 65 ter 1D54. And if we can focus on the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: This, Mr. Bushi, is a document that also my learned colleagues showed to you. It's a press release from the Security Council dated 7th of March, 2001. As you see, the title reads Security Council in presidential statement condemns violence by ethnic Albanian extremists in former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia. If we focus in the first paragraph the statements are related and I'm quoting the last line of the first paragraph. "In particular, the killing of three soldiers from that country in the Tanusevci area." Now, did you see that, Mr. Bushi, that they are referring to this particular event?

utterances.speaker: NAZIM BUSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: If we could go do Exhibit 1D231, please. It's former 65 ter 1D818. I believe that there is no Macedonian translation either.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Mr. Bushi, this is a document also shown by my colleagues dated the 30 of April, 2001. If we could go to page number 6, please. This briefing from the US State Department where the deputy spokesperson, Mr. Reeker is asked several questions. In particular, if we focus in the question that we see in the centre of the document a journalist is asking Mr. Reeker: "Does the attack on the security forces over the weekend and the NLA's claim of responsibility for it have an impact on what kind of message you will be hoping to see from President Trajkovski when he comes to visit tomorrow." Mr. Bushi, do you see that this question refers to an attack allegedly committed by the NLA against security forces of the Republic of Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: NAZIM BUSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: If we could go to Exhibit 1D232, please, the first page. It is former 65 ter 1D72.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Mr. Bushi, this is again another document which has been shown to you by my colleagues. It is a briefing from the Euro-Balkan Institute on Macedonian crisis and it's dated the 9th of May, 2001. We see in the first paragraph it reads, the first line: "In the Kumanovo village yesterday the most intensive combat by the Macedonian soldiers and policemen and Albanian terrorists took place." Do you see, Mr. Bushi, that this briefing is referring to a combat between the NLA and between Macedonian security forces, meaning soldiers, army and policemen?

utterances.speaker: NAZIM BUSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: If we go to Exhibit 1D227, please. Also the first page. It is former 65 ter 1D688. It is an article entitled: "Will Macedonia be next" from the Jane's Intelligence Digest and it is dated the 2nd of February, 2001. And if we can scroll down, please. In the first paragraph we see how the article is referring and I quote the second line: "In the space of a week, ethnic Albanian terrorists have launched an attack on a Macedonian police station." Mr. Bushi, do you see that this article is talking about an attack by the NLA against a police station, Macedonian police station?

utterances.speaker: NAZIM BUSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: If we could go to the second page of this document, please. We can see in the third full paragraph it starts: "The low level attacks against the Macedonian police which began last year are supposedly the work of the so-called liberation army." Mr. Bushi, do you see that this article is again referring to attacks committed by the NLA against Macedonian police forces?

utterances.speaker: NAZIM BUSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Thanks. We can remove this document from the screen. Mr. Bushi, do you recall yesterday that the pages 35 and 36 you were asked by my colleague about two helicopters and I believe that tanks and APCs which had been either shot down or destroyed by the NLA. Do you recall being asked about that question?

utterances.speaker: NAZIM BUSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Mr. Bushi, would you agree that all the documents that I showed to you are referring to clashes between the Macedonian security forces and the NLA?

utterances.speaker: NAZIM BUSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Mr. Bushi, in page 5783 you mention that you met with a British captain who you believe was a NATO representative and you met him in Nagustak village. Do you recall providing that evidence, Mr. Bushi?

utterances.speaker: NAZIM BUSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is true.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: When did you meet with him?

utterances.speaker: NAZIM BUSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met with him during the negotiations for the Ohrid Agreement and the disarmament during the first, second, and third phase. I don't recall the exact date, but I think it must have been in August.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: And which was the purpose of this meeting? You already mentioned that it was the negotiations for the Ohrid Agreement and the disarmament. Which was the exact purpose of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: NAZIM BUSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The exact purpose of that meeting was they had been before in Sipkovica at the General Staff, Gezim Ostreni and Ali Ahmeti had met with them and they were sent to Nagustak village to meet me, the commander of Brigade 114, to discuss the -- the first, second and third disarmament phase.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Thanks. Mr. Bushi, do you recall being asked yesterday also by my colleague why you didn't mention in your statement, the statement that you gave in 2004 and you signed in 2006, why you didn't mention that among the security forces who arrested you there were Lions, members of the Lions unit. Do you recall being asked that question, Mr. Bushi?

utterances.speaker: NAZIM BUSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this moment, maybe I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Okay. Well, it is in page 5895 of the transcript. Mr. Bushi, when you were giving your statement in 2004 and when you sign it in 2006, do you recall being asked when you had seen the Lions unit for the first time in Macedonia, if you recall, Mr. Bushi.

utterances.speaker: NAZIM BUSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Lions I saw for the first time with my own eyes directly when I was arrested.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bushi. You testified about that. But my question is, do you recall whether in 2004 when you were giving your statement if you were asked this question?

utterances.speaker: NAZIM BUSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall it, to tell you the truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Thanks. Do you recall if the Prosecution asked you at that time whether among the security forces who arrested you were members -- which were actually the security forces, the units who arrested you, do you recall if the Prosecution asked you these questions in 2004? If you recall.

utterances.speaker: NAZIM BUSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall it, whether I was asked this question. But the fact is that two persons were arrested in Karadak area. They were hostages of the NLA but were released later.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Could we please go to Exhibit 1D230. It is former, again, 65 ter 1D54, and if we could go to page number 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: This is again, Mr. Bushi, it is the press release from the Security Council dated, I believe, the 7th of March 2001. If we could go to the bottom of this document. In this -- in this press release there are statements from members of different states. In this case we see James B. Cunningham from the United States who is making a statement. If we could go please to the next page. And we see in the top of this document that Mr. Cunningham in the last two lines of the first paragraph is defining it, is talking about the Macedonian Republic and I quote what he says: "Macedonia is an example of democracy based on the Rule of Law and Inter-ethnic Cooperation." Mr. Bushi, would that description of the Macedonian government be an accurate statement, accurate description before 2001, before the conflict?

utterances.speaker: NAZIM BUSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Could we please go to 65 ter 1011.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Your Honours this is a book entitled, The war in Macedonia in 2001, which has been written by three Macedonian members of the -- Generals Mr. Arsovski, Kuzev and Damjanovski, and if we could go first to the title, so we can see the title of this book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, we don't want to interrupt but if my colleague had a paper copy of the document that'd be helpful. We were not warned that this would be -- and we're happy to go on with the book, but if there is a paper copy we can seep through, we would be grateful.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Let me check. We don't have it right now, but we will show to you on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: This is the title, Mr. Bushi. And if we could to in the English version within the range N006-3325, N006-334, to page 1. And within the Macedonian version it will be page 404. Your Honour, sorry for the interruption. I have just been informed that this document will be used with the next witness so we can provide you with a part of the binder that we have prepared for the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, it is the last tab of this binder. Your Honours, we're going refer to a few pages of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I'm grateful to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: We will provide to Your Honours the binders for Mr. Viktor Bezruchenko's testimony. If we could focus in item 2, we see that the paragraph starts: "The main causes of the escalation of the crisis and the outbreak of the war in Macedonia were the long-standing illusory peace; the conviction that Macedonia was an oasis of peace and not a powder keg; the live illusion that the ethnic tensions had relaxed or been resolved; the conviction that democracy was progressing apace; the belief that all citizens had been given all civil rights." Mr. Bushi, the belief that this document is talking about that in 2001 there were not ethnic tensions and that all civil rights were fully respected was as this text suggests, in fact, an illusion?

utterances.speaker: NAZIM BUSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Thanks. Now if we focus in the same paragraph just four lines in the bottom. Still also in the same page in the Macedonian version, we can read in the centre of the paragraph: "All decisions in Macedonia were made after prior agreement between the governing parties which most often expressed the particular interests of their party, not those of the state as a whole." Mr. Bushi, is this an accurate description of the Macedonian political scenario in 2001?

utterances.speaker: NAZIM BUSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: If we could go to page 4 of the English version and it will be page 408 of the Macedonian.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Mr. Bushi, in the Macedonian version is actually the last four lines of the paragraph, of the whole page and then we will have to move to the next page. We're actually talking about item 9. And if we could scroll up in the English version. In the centre of this paragraph, we can read: "In view of the fact that the state's security was disrupted on a larger scale, the Ministry of Defence and the Ministry of Interior," and I believe that in the Macedonian we have to move to the next page. "The Ministry of Defence and the Ministry of the Interior objectively had a prominent rule before and during the war. The one thing they had in common was that they operated separately with little or no coordination. In fact, they hardly seemed to be bodies belonging to the same state at all." Mr. Bushi, is this an accurate description how the government was working in 2001?

utterances.speaker: NAZIM BUSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is an accurate description, and I have mentioned this in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: If we could in the English version, please, scroll down. And then in the Macedonian version we have to -- now we keep this page and then we will move. If we focus also now in item 11. The fifth line starting from the beginning reads: "But seeing that they brought coalition government, involved parties with opposing interests, the two powers of the Macedonian security forces remain under the command of personalities with different political allegiances. The Macedonian army and police, therefore, conducted separate armed operations, independently of each other, without any joint plan for a specific and synchronised armed operations." Mr. Bushi, is this also an accurate reflection of how the government was working in 2001?

utterances.speaker: NAZIM BUSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is an accurate and realistic description.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Could we go to page 5 of the English translation and page 411 of the Macedonian. Mr. Bushi, do you recall being asked by my learned colleague about the fact that the NLA was not involved in the negotiations in the signing of the Ohrid Agreement, that was in pages 5827 or pages 5925, and you answered that the Albanian parties came up or produce what was orchestrated by Mr. Ali Ahmeti. I believe that those were your words. Do you recall that evidence, Mr. Bushi?

utterances.speaker: NAZIM BUSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Now, in item 13, we can read in the first line and I quote: "The influence of the international community on the final outcome of the war was significant." And then if we move to the centre of the paragraph, five lines below it reads: "Via its institutions and missionaries (facilitators) the international exerted excerpted unprecedented pressure on Macedonia, thus playing into the hands of the Albanian factor in the Balkans. The NLA, through its well prepared political representatives, succeeded in foisting its demands on the international community ..." Now if we could go to page 6 of the English version and page 412 of the Macedonian version. It will be item 15. The next page in the Macedonian version, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: The first five lines of this paragraph read: "The best thing to come out of the war was the Ohrid Framework Agreement. It shows and proves that the war was arranged and was meant to be waged for as long as it took the Macedonian government to agree to negotiate the demands of the NLA in the name of the Macedonian people." Mr. Bushi, do these statements reflect the role that the NLA play in the negotiation process of the Ohrid Agreement?

utterances.speaker: NAZIM BUSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Now, if we focus in item 14 of the same page. If we can scroll up the English version. The paragraph starts and I quote: "According to all indications from the analysis of the war we can conclude that it was planned, well organised and strictly controlled." Now if we go three lines below we can read, and it is referring to both parties of the conflict and I quote: "For this it had prepared corresponding measures for strict control of the military activities of both sides. Control was exercised and put into effect using a dosage of forces, a strict channelling of military activities, losses planned in advance, and military activities that took place in agreed operations." Mr. Bushi, is this text an accurate reflection of the conflict of Macedonia and the role played or the modus operandi of the NLA in the conflict?

utterances.speaker: NAZIM BUSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think no.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: How would you describe, then, the role play, or do you want me to repeat the text?

utterances.speaker: NAZIM BUSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The war was not planned and controlled by the two sides. It was controlled by our side. We had a well established military hierarchy.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Thanks, Mr. Bushi. I believe that you can speak for your side, meaning the NLA, and my question was actually with regards to your side, the NLA.

utterances.speaker: NAZIM BUSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... This text reflect the NLA role in the conflict, the modus operandi in the conflict, in general terms?

utterances.speaker: NAZIM BUSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as far as NLA is concerned, yes. It had control over the war, and it had a hierarchy that it respected.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Thanks, Your Honours, I have nothing further. Your Honours, I forgot I would like to MFI this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, it will be P464, MFI.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Bushi, you will be pleased to know that concludes the questions for you. The Chamber would thank you for your -- the considerable time that you've been here in The Hague and the assistance that you have been able to offer. And you may now, of course, return to your ordinary activities. Thank you again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I see two faces. It's Mr. Saxon, is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time the Prosecution will call Mr. Viktor Bezruchenko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Apostolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. We have the military political expert present here, Mr. Blagoja Markovski engaged by the Defence counsel of Mr. Johan Tarculovski. He is a doctor in military political science and I would therefore ask the Court that he be allowed to follow the examination of this witness in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, that will be permitted, Mr. Apostolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm wondering if my learned colleague could simply provide the name again of the expert witness so that it comes up clearly in the transcript. Because it didn't come up clearly in the English version. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] His name is Dr. Blagoja Markovski. This is the name of the military and political expert. I would ask the court usher to lead this person in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Bezruchenko.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you please stand and read aloud the affirmation that is shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down. Mr. Saxon has some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And perhaps before we begin, we have some binders for the Trial Chamber and I believe also two for the accused. Your Honours, because of the size of Mr. Bezruchenko's report, in the interests of speed, I will probably not rely too much on the e-court system in terms of moving from page to page. I believe everyone in the courtroom should have their hard copies of the amended expert report and the amended addendum with them. And we have also brought hard copies of the Macedonian translation of the original version of the report, which is quite similar to the amended version so that the accused are able to follow along quickly in their own language. The binders being given to you now just contain some documents that I will review with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Sir, your name is Viktor Bezruchenko. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, my name is Viktor Bezruchenko.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bezruchenko, you tend to be a little bit soft-spoken. I just want to remind you that today you need to speak in a loud and booming voice so that everyone in the courtroom, including the interpreters can hear you.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I will do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And also I should tell you that you and I speak and we understand the English language, one of the many languages that you speak. We need to be careful that we don't overlap our conversation, and that we pause a moment between my questions and your responses, because if we don't do that we will like life very difficult for the interpreters who are working very hard behind us. Is that all right?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: That's perfectly all right, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You probably don't have to sit so close to the microphone, but it is up to you. You were born in 1953 in Moscow, Russia?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And you entered the military institute in Moscow in 1974, right?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And Your Honours, if you could turn, please, to tab 1 in the binder in front of you. This is Rule 65 ter number 368. It is the curriculum vitae of Mr. Bezruchenko. It has ERN number R062-9449 in English. And, Mr. Bezruchenko, you graduated from the military institute in Moscow in 1980.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And can you please describe briefly your main courses of study there.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: My main courses of studies included operations, tactics, military history, subjects related to military hardware, and English.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And did you also study the field known as war studies?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: Yes, basically this is what war studies encompass.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. And did you -- have you also earned post-graduate degrees?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you describe those degrees?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: I earned a Ph.D. in political studies from Moscow -- sorry, from Kiev University and I also have a master's degree in political studies from the University of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, when you joined the -- when you entered the military institute in Moscow, at that point were you a member of the Armed Forces of the Soviet Union?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, sir. This was counted as active service in the armed services of the Soviet Union.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And when you graduated in 1980, did you graduate with a particular rank?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I graduated with the rank of second lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And during the years 1980 to 1983, you were a staff officer with the Soviet General Staff in Moscow. Is that right.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: That's right, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And among other things you helped plan combat training exercises?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You also served as a staff officer and military translator in the Kiev air force engineering academy in the mid-1980s. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And did you also have experience during the 1980s as United Nations military observer?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honours. I was a member of the United Nations Truce Supervision Mission in the Middle East. I served in Sinai, in Cairo and in Syria.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Between 1988 and 1990 you were a senior military instructor at Kiev University. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Between 1990 and 1992 you were a senior officer and the director of foreign relations now with the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Ukraine. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Now during 1992 and 1993, did you serve for a time in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I served with the United Nations protection force in the capacity of the Chief of Staff of Sector Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What was your rank at that time?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: Colonel, full colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And after that position ended, what did you do then?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: I returned to Ukraine upon completion of the tour of my duty. I was appointed the chief of the peace keeping operations department of the General Staff of Ukraine in which I served for about seven months.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And when you left that position as the chief of the peace keeping operations department, where did you go from there?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: I received a job offer from the United Nations mission in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I accepted this offer and I was assigned to a post of a civil affairs/political officer in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So when you took that post -- and what year would that have been?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: That would have been early 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And at that time, then, did you retire from the army of the Republic of Ukraine?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So at that point you were now working as a civilian?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And then how many years did you spend in Bosnia-Herzegovina in this position?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: Well, I actually served in a number of positions in Bosnia-Herzegovina and, well, essentially this time span would be measured between 1994 and 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And when did you -- at some point did you become the chief of the policy and planning unit?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: That's right, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Was that for UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: In fact, UNPROFOR ceased to exist following the Dayton Peace Accords and the mission was transformed into the United Nations mission in Bosnia, UNBiH. And at this point of time, I indeed was made the chief of the policy and plans unit for this mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And when did you come to work for the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: In 2003, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And you continue to work for the Office of the Prosecutor until the present day, right?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And what is it your title and position here working for the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: My title and position at the Office of the Prosecutor is military analyst.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And can you just briefly describe what that role entails. What are your responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: Essentially, this role entails providing military dimension to organisations, individuals and events related to an armed conflict or a war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What do you mean by providing military dimension. I don't understand what that means.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: Well, essentially that means that military -- I'm doing military analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: Which covers or may cover such areas as structure and armament of the armies or warring parties involved in the conflict. Their organisations, factions, command and control issues, strategy tactics, operations on the ground, and such functional issues as operations, logistics, security, finance, training and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Just before you continue, Mr. Saxon. Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I think Mr. Saxon was about to tell Mr. Bezruchenko the same thing as I am which is Mr. Bezruchenko appears to be reading from a document and I think he should be invited to close the binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I agree with my colleague would you please close that binder in front of you, Mr. Bezruchenko.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And you speak the following languages, Mr. Bezruchenko: Ukrainian, Russian, English, French, what we refer to here as B/C/S, Macedonian, and Amharic. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honours. Well, --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I just need that a yes or no answer.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time I would seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is will be Exhibit P465.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, did there come a time when the Office of the Prosecutor tasked you with researching and writing a report regarding the events in Macedonia in 2001?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And -- you might want to sit back a little bit from the microphones, Mr. Bezruchenko. And can you briefly describe what your task was, what were you asked to do?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: Well, essentially, I was tasked to cover the issues related to conflict in Macedonia in 2001. And these issues would include structure --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Structure of what?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: Of -- I would put it as warring parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: That is structure of the NLA, organisation of the NLA. Its regulations. Its tactics and operations, its control of territory. I was also tasked to cover similar issues for the government security forces, I mean the government of the Republic of Macedonia, including the army, and the Ministry of Interior or, rather, Ministry of Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, if you can turn please to tab 2 in your binder -- well, actually, I believe Your Honours and my co-counsel have hard copies of the amended expert report of Mr. Bezruchenko. Can we provide a copy of our court binder to Mr. Bezruchenko or does he already have one? Yes, please. And this document, if we can pull it up from e-court. It's dated 13 September, 2007 and it has ERN number 5090 A-N006-5286.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, apart from the structure and organisation and operations of the NLA and the security forces of the Macedonian government, were you also tasked to research and write something about the events in Ljuboten in August 2001?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: That's right, sir. I was tasked to provide the essential summary of events in and around Ljuboten, covering three days in August 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Bezruchenko, can you describe, please, the different source materials that you reviewed to compile your report, your amended expert report?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: The source material which I reviewed while compiling my report can be subdivided into several groups. Group one would make the Macedonian government documents, including the documents of the Ministry of Defence and the documents of the Ministry of Interior. These would include various operational reports, orders, maps. Speaking specifically of the Ministry of Interior, these documents would also include the reports related to Operation Ramno. The next group would be made up of the NLA documents. Yet another group would make the documents of various international agencies and organisations, including NATO and various NGOs. And the -- finally, another group would also include various media reports, international media and local media.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Bezruchenko, in your amended expert report you used the phrase "armed conflict" from time to time and I just want to clarify this with you. When you use this phrase "armed conflict," are you referring to -- to the legal sense of this term or a military sense of this term?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: I'm referring to the military sense of this term, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. From a military perspective, what do you mean when you refer to the phrase or use the phrase "armed conflict?"

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: There are many definitions of an armed conflict. One which is, to my mind, the best in terms of reflecting the reality is the one which is provided by Jane publication GP 1-2 of the United States MOD and this definition says that an armed conflict is in fact an armed struggle or a clash between nations or groups within a nation. A conflict is normally of protracted nature, it involves use of arms and weaponry and is normally waged for attainment of certain military or political goals.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And if we can, and do you have a copy of your amended expert report with you? Perhaps in the other binder. No. The other binder. Not in that binder, in the other binder that you brought?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: Yes, I do, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we could turn, Your Honours, to what is actually the second page of Mr. Bezruchenko's amended expert report. And it's the page where the table of contents begins.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Are you there, Mr. Bezruchenko, are you with me?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'd like to briefly review with you the structure of your report, please. You started out, section 1, you provide an executive summary of your research and analysis. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Section 2 provides your research and analysis with respect to the National Liberation Army, or the NLA. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Section 3 provides an analysis of the government security forces. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Including the army of the Republic of Macedonia and the Ministry of Internal Affairs?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Section 4 is a summary of the events related to Ljuboten. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And what is the fifth part of your report?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: The fifth part of my report is the chronology of events in Macedonia during the period of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And when you say "the chronology of events," are you specifically relating to the events of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honours, the events of the conflict between January and October, September/October 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time I would seek to tender the amended expert report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, simply for -- as a matter of clarification from the Office of the Prosecutor we understand the law of the Tribunal to be that a party seeking to tender a particular expert report or expert analysis by one of its witness would only be entitled to seek to tender that part or those parts of the report which have been put to the witness. And as an authority for that proposition I will just cite the Milutinovic order on procedure and evidence of the 11th of July, 2006, paragraph 7. The same is true of the documents from this authority which makes the point that: "Sources or material upon which an expert witness has been compiling his or her report cannot be admitted wholesale," I'm quoting, "but only those parts or those documents which have been put to the witness." And I would simply like to clarify or to, in any case, make the record here that we understand that only those parts and those documents which Mr. Saxon proposes to put to the witness in his examination in chief will be tendered by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do not believe that the authority that my colleague cited from the Milutinovic case is the general practice of this Tribunal or even the practice so far in this trial. I'm referring to the expert reports previously admitted from Drs. Eichner and Stein. Second of all, the -- with respect to documents, so the Prosecution would certainly seek to have the entire report admitted rather than go through what is nearly 200 pages of text with this witness. With respect to documents, Your Honour, the position of the Prosecution is it does not seek to tender all of the documents that are reflected in the footnotes to the report of Mr. Bezruchenko because quite frankly, Your Honour, that would obviously create an enormous amount of additional exhibits, so we will not intend to do that. I have selected certain documents that Mr. Bezruchenko uses in his report and some other relevant documents which I will put to him today and I will ask that those documents, approximately 30 of them, be admitted into evidence. For the convenience of the Chamber and the parties, the Prosecution has created a DVD containing every single document that Mr. Bezruchenko refers to in the footnotes of his amended expert report and the amended addendum to his expert report. We do not propose to tender this DVD into evidence, but we would like to provide it to the Chamber, to provide it to the Defence so the parties will have this material available in case they want to refer to anything cited to in Mr. Bezruchenko's report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is the position able to be summarized, Mr. Saxon, that you would invite the Chamber to receive the whole of the report as such, as though you had referred the witness to each part of it, but that you do not seek to tender any of the documents referred to in the report, which have in various ways, perhaps, been relied upon by the witness, and will tender those upon which you specifically rely separately.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour. We will specifically rely on a number of those documents during the direct examination and if I can just simply, just for the sake of completeness, the same would be true for the amended addendum to Mr. Bezruchenko's report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I'm grateful to Your Honour. The first thing I would wish to do which appears not to have been picked up by the transcript, mention the date of the order in question from the Milutinovic Chamber which is the 11th of July of 2006. And in reply, Your Honour, I would wish to do no more than read the passage in question which is very clear. The Chamber said this: "As a general rule, the Trial Chamber will only admit those parts of the report and further material that is put to the expert during his oral testimony. The sources used by an expert witness in compiling his or her report will not be admitted wholesale. Expert reports should, however, be fully referenced in order to facilitate the Chamber's determination of their probative value and, ultimately, the weight to be ascribed to them." And I would respectfully submit, Your Honour, that the Prosecution has not responded to this matter. This is the position of the Tribunal as we understand it in relation to expert reports. And I believe contrary to what Mr. Saxon has suggested in relation to Mr. Eichner and Stein, the relevant passages of their report were, in fact, put to those witness. And we understand that the same practice and the same course should be followed in relation to this particular witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you, in fact, taking the position that Mr. Saxon should spend the time of going through each paragraph of the report with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, we don't think this should be a paragraph by paragraph exercise. We would spend way too much time doing so. But we believe that each section and Mr. Bezruchenko has been careful to subdivide the report in many different ways to the extent that the Prosecution seek to rely on any particular sub-section of the report be they in relation to the NLA or be they in relation to the Macedonian forces or any other part of the expert's report. We believe that the Prosecution should, as the Chamber suggested, put at least the content of those finding, as well as the basis upon which the witness has relied upon to come to his conclusion to the witness to permit, among other things, the Defence to challenge these findings or the basis of it, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We have, Mr. Saxon, an issue of completing practicalities. I do not believe it is founded in any Rule or legal principle that binds us. It is the normal practice of the Tribunal to resist unnecessary documentation and in particular to resist that when a report is received in evidence from a witness that there comes with it, included in it all the material relied upon by the expert, partly because that would, in most cases, be unnecessary, and, secondly, because it would be unfair to the Defence. So with regard to the attachments or the documents referred to, we will be clear, and your own motion has made it clear, that we are not dealing with those. The other issue concerns the report itself. And there the question is, are there parts of it that you do not rely upon, and if so, they can be identified and put to one side. The other issue, then, is if you don't go through every part of it, the Defence will need in their cross-examination, to go at least to those parts with which they disagree, whether you have specifically referred to them in your examination or not. Now, from the point of view of this Chamber, we see little to be practically gained by you rehearsing with the witness every paragraph on which you rely simply to have the witness say yes, that is my opinion as set out in that report. That is simply taking time. But it has got to be clear to the Defence what it is that you really are relying on so that they have an opportunity then to deal in cross-examination with the material parts of the report. Do you understand the competing interests?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour. Let me give a very brief response. It is -- the Prosecution seeks to rely on every part, if I can use the term part, of Mr. Bezruchenko's report, and with leave of the Chamber, then, I will briefly go through the major parts of the report with the witness, if the Chamber deems that to be necessary at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber is of the mind, Mr. Mettraux, and Mr. Saxon, that it would not be necessary for Mr. Saxon to take the witness to each part of the report in view of his expressed indication that he relies upon the whole of it. Mr. Saxon should and is free to, but not under compulsion to, go with the witness to parts upon which either he sees as a particular importance or which he feels need to be developed or explained in some particular way. But can it be very clear so that both yourself and Mr. Apostolski are clear that we would be minded to receive the whole report on the basis of the express indication that the whole of it is being relied upon, so that if you dispute or challenge parts of it, you should feel that it is necessary to go to those. Now we're not doing what we have suggested in any way to disadvantage you. We're doing it simply to save time because the report speaks for itself and if it's not further developed by the witness, what stands in the report clearly will stand in evidence so that you know exactly what it is that have you to answer. And if you dispute therefore some part of it, or wish to explore further some part of it, you should. Is that clear enough?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I'm grateful for the indication, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You will, I'm reminded by Judge Thelin that it would be helpful to point out as well that if -- even though the witness does not turn or refer to and Mr. Saxon does not tender any particular source, if in your view, that source is unreliable or does not support something that is in the report, you of course are free to and it would be appropriate for to you deal with that in cross-examination. Now, Mr. Saxon, you move for the admission of the report without anything else. The report and the addendum will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the report will be Exhibit P466; the addendum will be Exhibit P4661.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm grateful to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Sorry, a little correction. The addendum will be Exhibit P466.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, if you could turn, please, to page 11 in the English version of your amended expert report. This is -- we'll turn to paragraph 44. And this is page 13 in the Macedonian version.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: I'm with you, sir, paragraph 44.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And again, we're in section 2 which is the section related to the NLA. In paragraph 44, the first sentence reads: "NATO sources assessed the NLA as a well armed, well disciplined and highly motivated organisation that enjoyed the support of the ethnic Albanian population. On a tactical level, the NLA was clearly disciplined, organised and maintained a marked superior level of morale over the Macedonian security forces." Then in the last sentence of that paragraph you write: "Though NLA capabilities were limited, it was assessed to be sufficient to face down the ill-coordinated, badly executed efforts of the Macedonians." Do you what I've written?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: In a broad military sense, based on your training and experience, how would you describe in general the fighting capabilities of the NLA during the summer of 2001?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: During the summer of 2001, the NLA had about six brigades on the ground. These brigades were of varying strengths. And it had sufficient weapons to arm these brigades. Its tactics included tactics of asymmetrical warfare which include raids, ambushes, and attacks on the soft targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, I need to stop you there. What do you mean by soft targets?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: Well, I mean the targets which would be relatively easy to attack at a low cost of casualties and inflict sufficient damage to the adversary.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Were the NLA forces capable of carrying out certain operations?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's right. As is evident from the chronology of my report, they were indeed numerous operations of this kind which were carried out by the NLA forces.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters kindly ask that the Prosecution speak closer to the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I apologise. I will try to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you can turn, please, Mr. Bezruchenko, to what is section -- part of section 3 of your report. It is page 106 in the English version and page 95 in the Macedonian version. And you see, Mr. Bezruchenko, are you with me on page 106?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: That's right, sir, I am with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And we see a subheading 3.3.3, called the Ministry of Internal Affairs command and control system. And then we see paragraph 369, says this: "The command and control relationship between the minister of the interior and the ministry's employees, emanates from Article 6 of the law," and you're referring to the Law on Internal Affairs, "which makes it mandatory for all employees of the ministry to carry out orders of the minister with the caveat for orders that would result in a criminal offence." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Help us, please. What does Article 6, then, of the Law on Internal Affairs tell us about the minister's place in the chain of command of the Ministry of Internal Affairs?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: Well, this is very clear. As in any military or police hierarchical organisation, well, according to the basic principles of command and control there should be one person in charge of an institution and this person is the minister. He is the one who is ultimately responsible for all operations, actions of the ministry, as well as his subordinate personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: We wish to let the witness answer this question before objecting but simply for the record we'll mark it that this question and the answer goes beyond the expertise of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Nothing is called for, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Then I will continue, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you could turn, please, Mr. Bezruchenko, to what is page 114 in the English version. This is page 102 in the Macedonian version. In middle of page 114 there's subtitle, 3.3.3.4. titled, The minister's powers in a war or emergency situation. And paragraph 415, you speak about the specific powers available to the minister in special situations, such as war or emergencies, stipulated by Article 11 of the Law. Which Law are you referring to here, please?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: Here I'm referring to the Law of Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And you quote Article 11 of this Law here. And it says: "In order to protect the security of the Republic of Macedonia under conditions of war or emergency, or should the public order or tranquility be violated on a larger scale, it says the minister may organise police units in charge of performing specific tasks by policemen and candidate policemen," et cetera. And then below that, next paragraph: "Individuals as per paragraph 1 of this article shall be considered authorised officials." Do you see what you've written there?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: How does this paragraph, paragraph 415, relate to -- actually, let me step back a little bit. There's a term that -- I'd like to ask you if you can define a term for me, please. The term is "operational control."

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: Well, according to the concept of operational control, a commander who is responsible to carry out a certain mission must exercise his authority to organise, deploy and direct his forces in operational sense. That is, to make sure that this mission is accomplished. Normally, operational control does not include such issues as discipline, logistics -- and logistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And when you say, "normally operational control does not include such issues as discipline, logistics -- and logistics," for example, the aspect of discipline, who would be expected, if not the commander, to exercise operational control with respect to discipline?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: That would be -- these powers would be granted to the next superior of the commander who would have the operational control of his troops on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You said the next superior. Do you mean the superior below the commander?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: Well, not necessarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: Above the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters kindly ask that the Prosecutor use the other microphone as well when speaking to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I wonder, in view of that interruption and the time, whether this would be a convenient break.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It would, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And we will resume in half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, just before the break we were talking about disciplinary responsibilities and I just want to make sure that the record is clear. Let me ask you this: In a normal military structure, do superiors have disciplinary powers over their subordinates?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: Yes, of course they have, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And so, for example, hypothetically, if a captain of a military unit -- if a military operation was led by a captain and if disciplinary matters arose during the course of that operation, then afterwards who would be responsible for dealing with possible disciplinary problems?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: Well, normally, this issue would be addressed by somebody in the hierarchy up from this level.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Bezruchenko, part 5 of your report titled the chronology, does it refer to --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I see Mr. Mettraux is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't mean to interrupt Mr. Saxon in his question but I see he is moving on to a different section of the report, Your Honour, and before my colleague does that I would be grateful if he could indicate to the Defence in what part of the report of Mr. Bezruchenko is the issue or the theory of operational control which has been explored with the witness a moment ago before the break is being substantiated. I mean by that where the reference to the material which support this particular theory is to be found, I would be assisted.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, there is a section on operational control within the Ministry of the Interior, and it is at 3.3.3.1, starting at page 107 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I'm grateful to Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: In the chronology section of your report, Mr. Bezruchenko, part 5, do you refer to combat activities in which members of the Macedonian Ministry of the Interior took part?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we can turn, Your Honours and Mr. Bezruchenko, to what is at tab 5 in the binder in front of you, please. And this is Exhibit number P00381. Mr. Bezruchenko, this is -- actually, if we could turn first, please, to what is at tab 4, Mr. Bezruchenko, and this is Exhibit 1D0012. This is a document dated the 7th of March, 2001. It is signed by the minister of internal affairs at that time Mr. Dosta Dimovska. Do you see this Mr. Bezruchenko?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And it's a decision to form the headquarters of operative action Ramno. And it says: "In order to organise, manage, coordinate, and direct the measures and activities in connection with the operative action Ramno, headquarters are formed in the following composition." And then we see a number of members of the Ministry of the Interior listed below. Mr. Bezruchenko, what connection, if any, is there to this document in the use of police in combat during 2001?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: This document is dated 7 March 2001, and should be analysed in the context of the developments in Macedonia at that time. The situation on the border was pretty tense. There were armed clashes which started in January, in fact, and by March it was becoming obvious that certain commitment of forces would be necessary to stem the NLA. There is direct connection between this document and what was happening on the ground, and this document reflects the fact that a special headquarters was created in the Ministry of Interior to deal with the issue of the NLA.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters --

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: Apparently, this headquarters was receiving all the information from the police units on the ground which were involved in fighting.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters need to note that the sound volume of Prosecutor's microphone is significantly lower than those of other microphones and it creates difficulties for us, so we kindly ask that something is done about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I will try to keep my voice higher then. Perhaps that will assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we can turn Mr. Bezruchenko then to what is tab five in your binder. And this is Exhibit P381. Exhibit P381 dated the 29th of May, 2001. It is also a decision to form the headquarters of operative action Ramno. But this time it's signed by the then minister of the interior Ljube Boskoski. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: I see that, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, again, what would then the connection be between this document and the use of police forces in combat?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: This document is dated 29 May 2001. And the significance of this document is practically the same as that of the previous one. Again, the analysis of this document would demonstrate that the combat activities in Macedonia continued, and essentially the same measures as undertaken within Operation Ramno had to be carried on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Can you turn, please, to what is tab 6 in your binder, Mr. Bezruchenko, and this is a document -- this is 65 ter number 966.11. It's a telegram signed by the Minister of the Interior. It's dated 11 June 2001, and it's sent to SOI Kocani, sector of finances and other common matters and the sector for analytics and investigation. First of all just in general, Mr. Bezruchenko, the town of Kocani, what part of Macedonia is that located in?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: I can't tell you exactly, sir, where it is located, but I don't think it is located in northern Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, what part of Macedonia is it located in?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: Kocani Well, I would imagine in -- I simply don't know, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can -- can we show -- let me ask you the question in another way. In June of 2001, to your knowledge was there any combat activity going on around the town of Kocani?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: I assume not, sir, not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Then this document continue: "In order to undertake security forces in the territory of the Republic of Macedonia and replacement of the police forces, it is needed that on 12 June 2001, Tuesday, the latest until -- until -- no later than 0700 hours, 50 policemen and Sapelovski Mitko, their senior officer in charge, be transferred to the military barracks --" I apologise for my poor Macedonian, "Hristian Todorovski Karpos in Kumanovo." And then it says: "The police should be equipped with their own personal and formation arms, a military set of information, camouflage uniforms, terrain boots, a bullet-proof vest with a shield, a helmet," and later on it says, "a set for personal hygiene for a period of at least 15 days out in the field." Very briefly, if our court officer could pull up from e-court please what is ERN N006-3997. And, Your Honours, this is simply the map of Macedonia that is at page 2 of your Court binder. I'm grateful to Ms. Alvarez for her assistance. Can you see now on this map, Mr. Bezruchenko, where the town of Kocani is?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you see that it is located towards the eastern part of Macedonia, going towards the border with Bulgaria?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I discovered this morning that this very basic map has not yet been tendered into evidence and I would ask that it be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, it will be Exhibit P467.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we can turn back now to what is tab 6 in your binder, 65 ter number 966.11.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: We see the date of this document, 11 of June, 2001, and we see that the minister of the interior is directing that 50 policemen and their senior officer be transferred from the Kocani area up to the Kumanovo area. At that time, Mr. Bezruchenko, why were more security forces needed at Kumanovo?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: In June 2001, fighting was going on in the area of Kumanovo. In fact, the area of Kumanovo was the second front, which was opened by NLA sometime in May 2001. So I assume this document indicates that certain reinforcements or replacement of police forces in this area would be required.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What connection, if any, or relevance if any, do you see between this order or instruction by Minister Boskoski and the question of Mr. Boskoski's operational control over police forces?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: As I mentioned previously, the operational control involves matters related to organisation and deployment of the forces on the ground. So this is the document which was issued as an exercise of the operational powers by the minister of the interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: We have no objection to the document being admitted we object, however, to the evidence which is elicited from Mr. Bezruchenko which is beyond the realm of his expertise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The evidence is received.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: May I continue, then, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is will be Exhibit P468.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you could turn, please, to what is tab 7 in your binder, Mr. Bezruchenko.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, this is 65 ter number 966.10.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, you'll see this is another telegramme signed by the minister of interior, Mr. Boskoski. It's dated the 13th of June, 2001, and this telegramme is directed to SOI Bitola. And can you recall just in general terms where, roughly, in what part of Macedonia the town of Bitola is, north, south, east or west?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: Bitola is more to the south of Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And in June 2001, was there any combat activity going on around Bitola?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, not, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: This telegramme says: "In order to undertake security measures in the territory of the Republic of Macedonia and replacement of the police forces, it is needed that on the 14th of June," the next day "latest until 0730 hours, 20 policemen and their senior officers in charge be transferred to the premises of the territorial fire-fighting unit Tetovo driven in your vehicles." Again, the policemen should be equipped with their own personal and formation arms, military set of ammunition, camouflage uniforms, et cetera. Mr. Bezruchenko, at this period in the middle of June in 2001, what was going on around the Tetovo area, around the city of Tetovo?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: The area of Tetovo, in fact, presented the first front which was again opened by NLA sometime in March 2001. To be more precise, in fact on the 14th of March, 2001. And it has remained a hot bed of fighting for the entire period of the conflict. There was fighting going on there in June 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. And if I were to ask you the question I asked you earlier about the relationship of this document to the operational control of the minister, would you give me the same response?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I would give the same response. This document is essentially of the same nature as the previous one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I would seek to tender this document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, it will be Exhibit P469.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you could turn, please, to what is tab 8 in your binder, Mr. Bezruchenko.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, this document is 65 ter number 966.9.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And you'll see, Mr. Bezruchenko, that this document is dated 23rd June, 2001. Again, it's signed -- again, it is a telegramme from the cabinet of the ministry of internal affairs, signed by Ljube Boskoski. And it's directed to SOI Stip. And can you recall from your memory, Mr. Bezruchenko, roughly where the town of Stip is in Macedonia, in what part?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: As far as I recall, it is again more to the south of the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. And to your knowledge, in June of 2001, were there any combat activities going on in Stip?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And this directive says that: "In order to undertake security measures in the territory of the Republic of Macedonia and replacement placement of the police forces, it is needed that on 24 June 2001, the latest 0730, 50 policemen and their senior officers in charge be transferred to the military barracks in Tetovo, driven in your vehicles." And the same instructions are given in the second paragraph regarding the equipment that the policemen should bring. We also see a third paragraph saying: "Senior officers, before the departure of the units, are asked to conduct an inspection of the policemen's personal appearance and equipment." Mr. Bezruchenko, given the military context at the time, why was it important to transfer police officers from Stip to Tetovo?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: Again, since Tetovo has been a very active area militarily, I would imagine that certain actions would have been required to reinforce the security forces in the area or replace them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, again, if I asked you the same question that I asked earlier related to the connection between this telegramme and Minister Boskoski's operational control, would you give me the same response?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I would seek to tender this document, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, it will be Exhibit P470.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, I would ask you, please, to turn to what is tab 9 in your binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, this would be 65 ter number 966.8.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I am with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm waiting for the document to come up on the -- the screen. Mr. Bezruchenko, we see this is another telegramme signed by Minister Boskoski. It's dated the 17th of July, 2001. And it's directed to SOI Veles. Can you recall where the town of Veles is, or Titov Veles?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: I understand it more to south-east of Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. To the best of your knowledge, was there any combat activities taking place around Titov Veles in the middle of July 2001?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And in this first paragraph we see that by 0730 hours on the 18th of July, 40 policemen and their senior officers in charge were being transferred to the premises of the territorial fire-fighting unit in Tetovo. And again we see the same paragraph about the kind of material and equipment that these police officers should take with them. And, again, I don't mean to belabour the point, the relationship between this document and the activities in Tetovo, Mr. Bezruchenko?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO.
utterances.text: Well, this document is essentially of the same nature as the previous one. And obviously, there was tense and difficult situation militarily in July 2001 around Tetovo.
